title: SRE standards: SLOs, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, and runbooks
author: Ari Chen
body:
Summary:
This document defines Redwood Inference’s SRE standards for service-level objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning guidance, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling expectations, and canonical runbook templates. The goal is to provide a single reference that product, platform, and SRE teams can use to set measurable reliability targets, plan capacity, conduct consistent post-incident reviews, and maintain up-to-date operational runbooks.

Scope and audience:
- Applies to all public-facing and internal model-serving, routing, and storage services owned by platform, serving-runtime, and infra teams.
- Intended readers: SREs, service owners, product engineering leads, and incident commanders.

1) SLOs and error budgets
Overview:
- SLOs represent the customer-facing reliability target for a service. Each user-visible service must have at least one primary SLO and supporting secondary SLOs where appropriate.
- Error budgets quantify allowable failure and drive release and roll-out decisions.

Primary SLO definition rules:
1. Primary SLO must be defined for critical user journeys (examples: API availability for text generation, median 95th percentile latency for interactive chat, embeddings pipeline throughput).
2. Each SLO must include: objective (e.g., 99.9%), measurement window (rolling 30d by default), SLI definition (metric name and query), and owner.
3. Use user-impacting SLIs (request success rate, end-to-end latency, completeness of streaming responses) rather than purely internal metrics.

SLO examples (text table):
Service | SLI | Objective | Window | Owner
------- | ---- | --------- | ------ | -----
Model Serving API | request_success_rate (5xx/timeout) | 99.9% | 30d rolling | eng-serving-runtime
Chat Low-latency Tier | p95_latency (ms) for request_to_first_token | 300ms | 30d rolling | eng-serving-runtime
Embeddings Pipeline | batch_throughput_per_minute | >= 8 batches/min | 30d rolling | eng-platform

Measurement queries (examples):
- Success rate (PromQL):
  1 - sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="model-api",code=~"5..|504|599"}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="model-api"}[5m]))
- p95 latency (Histogram):
  histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="chat-lowlat"}[5m])) by (le))

Error budget policy:
- Error budget = 1 - objective. Track burn rate on a rolling 7d and 30d window.
- Thresholds and actions:
  - Normal: burn rate <= 1. No additional controls required.
  - Elevated: 1 < burn rate <= 3. Notify owners; pause non-critical launches.
  - Critical: burn rate > 3. Escalate to on-call lead, freeze feature rollouts for the service, and run a focused reliability initiative.
- Owners must publish remediation action plans when the 7d burn rate enters Elevated or Critical.

2) Capacity planning
Principles:
- Plan for peak traffic scenarios using a 99th-percentile forecast for traffic spikes relevant to the business (PLG growth, enterprise batch windows, regional events).
- Maintain measured headroom: target minimum of 25% usable capacity headroom for production clusters under normal operating load.
- Use real traffic traces and model-serving-specific characteristics (token rates, sequence length distribution, KV-cache hit rates) when simulating capacity.

Capacity planning lifecycle:
1. Forecasting: monthly forecast with inputs from metrics, product launch calendar, sales commitments, and historical growth rates.
2. Simulation: run perf-simulator against representative model versions and sequence length distributions. Capture latency/P95 and throughput tradeoffs.
3. Procurement and allocation: request additional GPU reservations or cloud capacity at least 6 weeks before predicted need for on-demand clusters; 12 weeks for reserved/dedicated capacity.
4. Verification: run canary traffic at new capacity; validate SLOs over a 72-hour verification window.

Capacity runbook (short checklist):
- Current utilization by cluster (token/sec, GPU util, avg sequence length).
- Current scheduled capacity changes (with ETA and owner).
- Pending product events (launches, marketing spikes).
- Action steps to add capacity (ordering process, terraform modules to update, runbook commands).

3) Reliability initiatives and prioritization
Reliability initiative definition:
- Multi-week projects (2-12 weeks) focused on measurably improving SLOs or reducing operational toil (examples: adaptive batching, KV-cache prefetch, improved quantization profiles).

Prioritization criteria:
- Expected SLO lift or error budget improvement (quantified).
- Impact on cost-per-token or operational cost.
- Risk reduction (reduces likelihood/severity of common incidents).
- Effort estimate and cross-team dependencies.

Initiative template (to be used in planning doc):
- Title
- Owner and team
- SLOs impacted and baseline metrics
- Success criteria (numeric target)
- Timeline and milestones
- Rollout plan and rollback criteria

4) Incident review standards (postmortems)
Requirements for all incidents meeting the incident threshold (SLA breach, P1/P0 service outage, or >24h degraded performance):
- Postmortem must be published within 48 hours of incident declaration start.
- Postmortem must include: incident summary, timeline of events, detection signal, mitigation steps, root cause analysis (RCA), action items with owners and due dates, and lessons learned.
- Severity levels and expectations:
  - P0/P1 (major outage): full RCA, service-level follow-ups, and 1:1 review with engineering leadership as needed.
  - P2 (significant degradation): focused RCA and action plan within 7 days.

Postmortem template (key sections):
1. Title and incident ID
2. Summary (what happened and customer impact)
3. Timeline (timestamped events)
4. Detection (how the issue was observed)
5. Immediate remediation steps taken
6. Root cause analysis and contributing factors
7. Actions (owner, due date, verification criteria)
8. Follow-up verification results
9. Related alerts/dashboards/runbooks referenced

Blameless review guidance:
- Focus on systems and process improvements, not individual fault. Encourage psychological safety and candid detail.

5) Operational tooling and observability expectations
Dashboards and alerts:
- Each SLO must have an associated SLO dashboard that includes SLI time series, error budget burn rate, top contributing error types, and traffic breakdown by region/model-version.
- Alerting policy should follow a tiered model: symptom alerts (customer-observable failure), cause alerts (infrastructure/host-level), and runbook alerts (clear link to runbook).
- Keep per-service alert counts reasonable: default max of 12 actionable alerts per service; alert fatigue reviews quarterly.

Tooling standards:
- Source-of-truth for runbooks: consolidated in Confluence under eng-sre runbooks and linked from service configuration.
- Incident timelines: use the centralized incident tracker (internal URL) and attach postmortems to the incident.
- SLO tracking: primary SLOs tracked in the SLO dashboard system (Grafana + internal SLO exporter).

Recommended observability queries and widgets (examples):
- SLO burn rate panel (7d and 30d)
- Top 5 error codes by count for the service
- p50/p95/p99 latency heatmap by region and model-version
- Queue/backlog length for offline pipelines

6) Canonical runbook templates (operational runbooks)
Runbook structure (required sections):
- Title and owner
- Symptoms (customer-observable indicators)
- Priority and impact classification
- Diagnostic steps (commands/queries with expected outcomes)
- Mitigation steps (short-term and long-term)
- Rollback and escalation paths (names and paging info)
- Post-incident validation and follow-up actions

Example runbook: Model Serving API (shortened)
- Title: model-serving-api - production response-time degradation
- Owner: eng-serving-runtime oncall rotation
- Symptoms: increased p95 latency > 400ms or error rate > 0.5% sustained for 10m
- Diagnostic steps:
  1. Check SLO dashboard and burn rate: Grafana -> SLO -> model-serving-api
  2. Query current error rates:
     sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="model-api"}[5m])) by (code)
  3. Check GPU utilization and queue length on serving cluster:
     kubectl -n serving get pods -l app=model-serving -o wide; check node GPU metrics
  4. Inspect recent deploys: CI/CD pipeline -> last 60 minutes
- Mitigation steps:
  Short-term:
  - Scale up serving pool by +10% (run terraform apply module=serving-cluster-scale var.size_delta=10) or trigger autoscale policy
  - Route traffic to fallback region/model-variant: update routing policy in the control plane (CLI: redwood route promote --service model-serving-api --variant fallback-v1)
  Long-term:
  - Create reliability initiative to reduce tail latency: adaptive batching, KV-cache tuning
- Escalation: page oncall lead (pager duty) if symptoms persist after 30 minutes
- Post-incident: attach metrics and timeline to the postmortem, open action items for verification

Runbook maintenance:
- Owners must review and sign-off their runbooks quarterly and after any relevant incident.
- Runbooks must include verification steps with expected metric checks (e.g., p95 < 300ms for 24h).

7) Governance and review cadence
- Quarterly SLO review: owners present SLO health and error budget usage as part of SRE sync.
- Reliability roadmap review: product and SRE review major reliability initiatives each planning cycle.
- Runbook audits: rotate audit ownership; each service must complete a runbook audit every 6 months.

Appendix A: Quick reference commands and queries
- Check current SLO burn rate (example CLI): redwood-slo-cli get-burn --service model-serving-api --window 7d
- Scale serving pool (example Terraform): terraform apply -var 'serving_pool_delta=2' modules/serving-cluster
- PromQL example (error rate): sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="model-api", code=~"5..|504|599"}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="model-api"}[5m]))

Appendix B: Related pages and templates
